etymologies.etymologyHTML: From a blend of smack +‎ mash. Compare Swedish smask (“to smack with the lips”), dialectal Swedish smaska (“to smack, kiss”), Danish smaske (“to smack with the lips”), Low German smaksen (“to smack with the lips, kiss”).

definitions.definition: The sound of a violent impact; a violent striking together.
(colloquial) Something very successful or popular (as music, food, fashion, etc).

quote.citation: 2007 June 26, Jackie Collins, Drop Dead Beautiful, St. Martin's Publishing Group, →ISBN, page 440:
2012 November 15, Tom Lamont, “How Mumford & Sons became the biggest band in the world”, in The Daily Telegraph‎[1]:
quote.text: […] Mumford & Sons – prospering British folk band, in the middle of a long tour of Australia, the US and the UK, their newly released album Babel a smash on all fronts – wander to centre stage.

quote.citation: 2019 May 1, Ginaluca Russo, “Taylor Swift Stuns In a Periwinkle Ruffle Mini Dress on the Billboard Music Awards Red Carpet”, in Teen Vogue‎[2]:
quote.text: All together, this look is a smash in our books.

definitions.definition: (tennis) A very hard overhead shot hit sharply downward.

quote.citation: 2011 July 3, Piers Newbury, “Wimbledon 2011: Novak Djokovic beats Rafael Nadal in final”, in BBC Sport‎[3]:
quote.text: A Nadal forehand into the net gave Djokovic the set and the Spaniard appeared rattled, firing a smash over the baseline in a rare moment of promise at 30-30 at the start of the third.

quote.citation: 1845, Basil Montagu, Edward Erastus Deacon, John Peter De Gex, Reports of Cases in Bankruptcy:
quote.text: Supposing a man has for the space of a month carried on trade in a showy shop in Cheapside, and then comes a smash, — is he not to be held a trader within the bankrupt law, because no one can swear that he has traded for four months?

definitions.definition: (colloquial, archaic) A disaster; a bad situation.

quote.citation: 1838, Boz [pseudonym; Charles Dickens], Oliver Twist; or, The Parish Boy’s Progress. […], volume (please specify |volume=I, II, or III), London: Richard Bentley, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: “There’s nowhere else to go to now, for the people at the Cripples are all in custody, and the bar of the ken—I went up there and see it with my own eyes—is filled with traps.”“This is a smash,” observed Toby, biting his lips. “There’s more than one will go with this.”

quote.citation: 2017, Charles Rawlings-Way, Brett Atkinson, Lonely Planet Discover Australia:
quote.text: […]  the saltbush dukkah, avocado and feta smash.

definitions.definition: A kind of julep cocktail containing chunks of fresh fruit that can be eaten after finishing the drink.

quote.citation: 2008, Tom Clancy, Chuck Horner, Every Man A Tiger‎[4]:
quote.text: Then, for Horner's red team, it became just a matter of gaining sufficient smash (airspeed) to convert on them and film them with gun cameras.

quote.citation: 1881–1882, Robert Louis Stevenson, Treasure Island, London; Paris: Cassell & Company, published 14 November 1883, →OCLC:
quote.text: I went back with him to the Admiral Benbow, and you cannot imagine a house in such a state of smash; the very clock had been thrown down by these fellows in their furious hunt after my mother and myself;  […]

quote.citation: 1857, Thomas Hughes, Tom Brown's School Days:
quote.text: The door panels were in a normal state of smash, but the frame of the door resisted all besiegers, and behind it the owner carried on his varied pursuits  […]

quote.citation: 1895 May 7, H[erbert] G[eorge] Wells, chapter X, in The Time Machine: An Invention, New York, N.Y.: Henry Holt and Company, →OCLC:
quote.text: Now, I still think that for this box of matches to have escaped the wear of time for immemorial years was a strange, and for me, a most fortunate thing. Yet oddly enough I found here a far more unlikely substance, and that was camphor. I found it in a sealed jar, that, by chance, I supposed had been really hermetically sealed. I fancied at first the stuff was paraffin wax, and smashed the jar accordingly. But the odor of camphor was unmistakable.

quote.citation: 2013 June 29, “High and wet”, in The Economist, volume 407, number 8842, page 28:
quote.text: Floods in northern India, mostly in the small state of Uttarakhand, have wrought disaster on an enormous scale. […] Rock-filled torrents smashed vehicles and homes, burying victims under rubble and sludge.

quote.citation: 2021 December 29, Dominique Louis, “Causal analysis: crashworthiness at Sandilands”, in RAIL, number 947, page 33:
quote.text: We also found that the only emergency egress from the tram was by smashing the front or rear windscreens, and that emergency lighting had failed when the tram overturned.

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To be destroyed by being smashed.
(transitive, figuratively) To ruin completely and suddenly.
(transitive, figuratively) To defeat overwhelmingly; to gain a comprehensive success over.
(transitive, US) To deform through continuous pressure.

quote.citation: 2016, Doreen Virtue, Jenny Ross, Veggie Mama, page 154:
quote.text: Using a fork, smash the avocado with all the remaining ingredients.

definitions.definition: (transitive, slang, vulgar) To have sex with.

quote.citation: 2020 November 7, Dave Chappelle on Saturday Night Live:
quote.text: Farmersonly.com. A website that begs the question, what kind of bitch only smashes with farmers?
In a leaked video, Keys also asked pundit Jamie Redknapp of an ex girlfriend: “Did you smash it?”

definitions.definition: (intransitive, slang, archaic) Synonym of go to smash (“to go to ruin; to fail disastrously”)

quote.citation: 1910, Fergus Hume, The Peacock of Jewels:
quote.text: "What would have become of the gems had the bank smashed?" asked Marie in a timid and rather tearful voice, for it was a terrible thought to think that her dreams might dissolve into thin air.

definitions.definition: (UK, Ireland, slang, obsolete) To pass counterfeit money.
